<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and format-compliant, and the debate narrowed cleanly to two questions: (1) does an opt-in signature actually change anything if it too is extracted under hiring pressure, and (2) does opt-in tax localization and cost dubbing work. CON's best moves — "the motion says dubbing, not deepfakes," the false-choice reframe toward collective bargaining, and "page 34 with a date" — genuinely pressured PRO. But PRO answered each on the decisive axis and kept control of the framing. The response that a discrete, dated, per-title, per-language grant is "priceable, scopeable, sunsettable" while an "all media hereafter devised" clause is invisible and unbounded meaningfully differentiates the two signatures; CON mostly asserted equivalence rather than refuting the scope distinction. PRO's absorption of CON's own best material was the pivotal reframe: every good term CON praised (disclosure, revocation, use limits, guild floors) presupposes that the studio needs something the performer has not already conveyed, so consent is the baseline bargaining exists on, not a rival to it. CON's rejoinder ("opt-in transfers the asset without transferring bargaining power") was cleanly flipped — transferring the asset is what a sale is, and page 34 is a giveaway. CON's strongest surviving route is the cost/market argument (raise friction and niche titles simply go undubbed), which remains live but was blunted by PRO's human-dubber fallback plus the "the interest served is a margin, not an audience" turn. CON also partly sidestepped PRO's Q2 about what protects the non-union day player, offering "guild floors, union or not," which is hand-wavy given CON's own reliance on bargained machinery. Enforcement symmetry was roughly a wash, with a slight PRO edge because policing a use presupposes a right to refuse it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's handling of CON's collective-bargaining reframe: conceding that negotiated machinery is better than a checkbox, then showing every such term only exists because the default answer starts at "no" — and flipping CON's "transfers the asset without transferring bargaining power" into "transferring the asset is the point of a sale; page 34 gave it away for nothing." That exchange converted CON's strongest structural argument into PRO's decision rule.</best_rebuttal>
